opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is that most of the digital world wasn't built for agents. It was built for humans — interfaces designed around eyes and a mouse, workflows that assume someone can glance at a page and intuitively understand what matters. So when an agent operates through a browser or a GUI, it's essentially reverse-engineering an interface meant for a different kind of user. APIs help, but coverage is patchy, and a huge amount of real value sits in systems that have no clean programmatic entry point at all.

The second limitation, and I'd say the more fundamental one, is long-horizon reliability. Calling a single tool correctly is mostly a solved problem now. But real tasks in the digital world are chains of dozens or hundreds of steps, and errors compound. If each step is 95% reliable, a fifty-step task almost always fails somewhere. What's missing is the ability to notice you've gone off track, backtrack, and recover — the kind of self-correction humans do almost unconsciously. That's less about tools themselves and more about the model's reasoning and its ability to maintain a coherent plan over a long context.

Third, there's the question of feedback and learning. Right now, a lot of tool-use capability comes from imitation — the model has seen examples of how things are done. But to truly control environments, you need agents that learn from interacting with them, through something like reinforcement learning in real or simulated environments. The bottleneck there is building environments that are rich enough and reward signals that are trustworthy enough. Many digital tasks don't have a clean "you succeeded" signal, so scaling that kind of training is genuinely hard.

And then finally there's trust and permissions. Even if the agent is capable, how much do you let it do? Sending money, deleting files, emailing on your behalf — these are irreversible actions. So part of the limitation isn't technical capability, it's designing the right boundaries so that humans are comfortable handing over control step by step.

So my view is that the path forward is a combination: stronger base models with better long-context reasoning, more training through interaction rather than just imitation, and gradually reshaping the digital world itself to be more agent-friendly. I think we'll see the environment and the agents co-evolve.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss tool-use benchmarks or say they fail to reflect actual user experience.

r003.rationale: It does not identify generalization to previously unseen or out-of-distribution tools as a challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that today's agents are still quite far from really "controlling the digital world," and the gap shows up in a few different places.

The first is reliability over long horizons. A single tool call, a model can do pretty well now. But a real task might involve dozens or hundreds of steps, and errors compound. If each step is ninety-five percent reliable, after fifty steps you're in trouble. So the bottleneck isn't whether the model knows how to call an API, it's whether it can stay on course, notice when something went wrong, and recover. That kind of self-correction is still weak.

The second is the interface itself. A lot of software was designed for humans, not for models. Browsers, GUIs, legacy enterprise systems, they have no clean API. So the agent has to operate through screenshots or DOM trees, which are noisy, slow, and change under your feet. I think over time the digital world will adapt to agents, the way the web adapted to search engines, but right now the agent is mostly meeting the world on the world's terms.

The third, and maybe the most fundamental, is that tool use requires a kind of world model. You need to predict what will happen when you take an action before you take it. A human clicking "delete" or "send" has an intuition about consequences. Models often don't. They act and then observe, rather than simulate first. That's fine in a sandbox and dangerous in production. It's also why we see agents do things that are locally reasonable and globally absurd.

Then there's the question of data. Pretraining data is mostly text describing the world, not records of acting in it. There's very little data of the form "here is a goal, here are the thousand decisions someone made to accomplish it, here's what worked." So the agent capability has to come largely from reinforcement learning, which means designing environments and rewards, and that's expensive and hard to generalize. You can get very good at the benchmark and still be fragile one step outside it.

And finally, I'd say there's a ceiling set by the model's own judgment. Tools amplify whatever the model is. If the reasoning is shallow, tools let it be shallow faster and at larger scale. So I don't think tool use is a separate module you bolt on. It's a test of whether the underlying intelligence is real. The limitations we see in agents today are mostly limitations in the base model's ability to reason, plan, and understand consequences, just made visible because now the model has hands.

astra-6.text:
I think one limitation is that being able to call a tool is very different from being able to reliably complete a task. An agent might use a browser correctly for a few steps, but a longer task requires it to maintain context, understand whether an action actually worked, and recover when something unexpected happens. Small errors accumulate, so reliability becomes much more important as the task gets longer.

There’s also a question of feedback. When you interact with the digital world, the result isn’t always a clear success or failure. The agent needs to understand what changed and whether that change brings it closer to the user’s goal. Sometimes the right next step is another action; sometimes it’s checking an assumption or asking the user a question.

So I would distinguish access from capability. We can give a model access to many tools, but that doesn’t automatically give it the judgment to use them well. The bigger challenge is making the whole loop—planning, acting, observing, and correcting—reliable enough that people can delegate meaningful work to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is reliability over long sequences of actions. An agent might be quite good at using an individual tool, but controlling a computer means connecting many steps: understanding the goal, choosing an action, interpreting the result, and deciding what to do next. A small mistake early on can change the situation, and the agent has to recognize that and recover. If it simply continues with its original plan, the errors accumulate.

There’s also a gap between knowing how something works and being able to operate it. A model may explain a piece of software very well, but when it encounters an unfamiliar interface or an unexpected response, that knowledge doesn’t always translate into the right action. So tool use is partly a reasoning problem, but it’s also a learning and feedback problem.

I think progress will depend on training agents on complete tasks, including failures and recovery, rather than only on examples of successful individual actions. The important question is whether an agent can reliably achieve an outcome, recognize when it hasn’t, and know when it needs help.
